title: Which Primitives an Agent activates is itself a public statement of strategy to its token holders
content:
A.2.2.1.2.1 states that an Agent may only Invoke a Primitive it has previously Globally Activated, and then draws out a second-order effect: "an Agent's decision regarding which Primitives to Activate allows the Agent to express its strategy to token holders." The worked example is an asset-gathering Agent that Globally Activates the Distribution Reward and Integration Boost Primitives but not the Allocation System Primitive.

What makes this a genuine signal rather than noise is A.2.2.1.2.3: "Activation gives the Agent the ability to Invoke a Primitive... but does not require the Agent to do so." Activation is therefore *costless in action* but *not costless in disclosure* — an Agent that activates a Primitive has announced that this capability is within its intended scope, whether or not it ever uses it.

The mechanism converts a permissions list into a legible strategy document. Token holders do not need to read an Agent's prose vision statement to see what it intends; they can read its activation state, which is machine-readable and lives in the Artifact.

It also creates a discipline: because post-launch activation requires a token holder vote and Operational Executor Facilitator review (A.2.2.1.2.4.1.3), an Agent that activates broadly to preserve optionality is signalling a wide mandate it must defend, while a narrow activation set is a self-imposed constraint holders can rely on.
description: Activation grants the ability to Invoke without obliging it, so the activated set reads as declared intent — an asset-gathering Agent activates Distribution Reward but not Allocation System.
